title: Coleman Hawkins: genius, 'Body and Soul' and his philosophy
summary: Wilson ranks Hawkins among a few geniuses, praises the continuity of 'Body and Soul', and relays Hawkins's belief that unplanned things matter most.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: We were talking about Coleman Hawkins before. Tell me something about you and -- you were talking about how he did that thing --

Yes, Coleman Hawkins was one of that little handful of very special, exceptionally talented people, Coleman Hawkins, Benny Carter, Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington, Art Tatum, these few who are far superior to the others in their

work. You know, they have an extra touch of genius and talent and most of these people, you find, are very individual in a way. They have sort of found themselves, their own path in life, and they're not pushed by every wave of the popular that comes and goes through the years, pushed from one side to the other like so many talented people. These people find themselves young, and they're on a path and they know it and they're just going straight ahead in their own way.

Like Hawkins, that tremendous ability he has. He's very unique. I thought that Coleman -- I used to work with him a few times, actually on tour, on the road working with him daily and making records. And I was very much influenced by his recordings, too. I learned a lot from his records along with my piano idols. And Coleman had the grand gift, I think, all this knowledge he had, it was always at his disposal. Anytime he picked up his horn, all this vast knowledge could be utilized, which to me is not so easy. Very often I know some things that I should have played that I didn't play. And Coleman, this tremendous mind he had, I think the continuity he showed in "Body and Soul" record, where every note logically follows the one before it, shows he almost could remember what he played from the first note on and relate all the following notes to the preceding notes. It called for a great deal of concentration and a tremendous grasp of music itself, to do that.

That solo is very unique that way, in an improvisation. And he had his own path. Once in a serious, philosophic discussion he told me he did not believe in things that you plan and work hard to achieve. Even if you get them, they're no good, he said. And they're not as good as what you thought they were going to be, and all the things over your life, he said, that really mean anything, the things that really are good for you, really good for you, are things you had no inkling they were going to happen. They come out of the clear blue sky with no warning at all. And those are the things that count.
So basically, if he's right, there's no need of planning. Just go with nature.
Yeah, right. And maybe he's right, you know. He sounded serious, he was very serious when he told me that.
